source.title: Meta-Weight-Net: Learning an Explicit Mapping For Sample Weighting
source.authors: Jun Shu; Qi Xie; Li-Xuan Yi; Qian Zhao; Sanping Zhou; Zong-Ben Xu; De-Yu Meng

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper trains networks on datasets with corrupted labels and reports training and test accuracy, which bears on V4; its primary intervention is learned sample reweighting, not the original random-label experiment.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Understanding deep learning requires rethinking generalization and A closer look at memorization in deep networks, but those cited results are not this paper's results. Figure 7 reports training and test accuracy curves for BaseModel, L2RW, and Ours; Appendix G describes BaseModel's overfitting. Other reported accuracy tables measure test accuracy of methods under corrupted labels, not fitting random labels.
record.test_reason: The unmodified BaseModel experiments use SGD, random label corruption, and training/test accuracy measurements, directly bearing on V4. The paper's main reweighting intervention does not determine the classification of these baseline experiments.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that learned sample weighting improves robustness under class imbalance and corrupted labels. Appendix G reports less noisy-label overfitting for MW-Net and L2RW than BaseModel, and faster convergence for MW-Net.
record.recipe_differences: The experiments use uniform or class-dependent label corruption and compare learned sample reweighting with baseline training; they do not reproduce training on wholly random labels.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset, corruption type and rate, classifier architecture, and training method vary across experiments.
record.problems: The relevant training and test accuracy curves are figure-only in the supplied text, with no stated numeric values; the paper does not explicitly state that the baseline reaches perfect training accuracy. Experiments concern partially corrupted labels, not fully random labels.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results retained. Main accuracy tables report test accuracy for methods under label corruption, but do not report the training-fit behavior named by V4.

untested.parts: Completely random labels, near-zero training error and chance test performance under that labeling, with unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Time to fit random versus real labels and convergence slowdown as corruption increases. Timing comparisons between reweighting methods do not test this.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
The full corruption sweep through 100% and the chance endpoint are not tested. Perfect whole-training-set fit at each corruption rate is not established by the supplied text.
Whether explicit regularizers prevent random-label fitting and whether removing them harms true-label generalization.
Separate learning trajectories for clean and corrupted examples establishing that shared real patterns are learned before noise. Aggregate test degradation alone does not establish this ordering.

record.verdict_notes: No directional verdict follows from R1–R4 because their curve values are unavailable and perfect training fit is not stated. Table 2 independently shows declining BaseModel test accuracy at 0%, 40%, and 60% uniform corruption: 95.60%, 68.07%, 53.12% on CIFAR-10 and 79.95%, 51.11%, 30.92% on CIFAR-100. This supports V4's degradation component, but those results are explicitly declared in rows_left_out and are not captured by the retained rows. Neither unreadable training curves nor incomplete corruption coverage constitutes a challenge or scope limitation.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not test completely random labeling of the training set, chance test error under that labeling, or fitting without changing architecture or training hyperparameters.
No comparison of time to fit completely random versus true labels, or convergence slowdown as corruption rises, is reported.
No shuffled-pixel, permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise input experiment is reported.

The paper tests uniform and class-dependent label corruption and plots training and test accuracy for several methods, but does not explicitly report perfect training accuracy across corruption fractions or steadily rising test error toward chance.

The paper compares sample reweighting methods; it does not test whether weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation prevent fitting random labels, or whether their removal harms true-label generalization.
The paper does not analyze whether true-label patterns are learned before noisy or random labels.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: The study reports its own baseline noisy-label overfitting and accuracy results at multiple corruption rates, bearing on V4.

tranche.reason: The BaseModel directly trains with SGD under independently randomized label corruption and measures training/test accuracy, matching the method and measures relevant to V4. The reweighting intervention does not replace these baseline experiments.

source_check.notes: BaseModel is WRN-28-10 under uniform noise. Figure 7 measures mini-batch training accuracy on noisy labels and clean-test accuracy; its extracted curves do not establish perfect training-set fit, and wholly random labels are untested.
